# Railtie Call Relationship Notes

This page started as a code-reading diagram posted next to `lib/newrelic_rpm.rb`. It placed Railtie after the file entry point, then placed initialization, failure, and event exits below Railtie. The usage was straightforward at the time: look for Railtie near the entry point first, then follow the three directions in order.

```text
lib/newrelic_rpm.rb
        |
     Railtie
        |
 Initialization / Failure / Event Exit
```

The old diagram was never removed. It is still useful when revisiting this existing rb module: the file entry point is clear, Railtie is the first object to look for, and initialization plus the two exits are terms to keep watching after reaching the relevant locations. The problem is that the diagram's layout looks like a completed call chain, so people later treated every vertical line as a direct relationship.

## How It Was Read at the Time

The initial reading was that Railtie connected the initialization action to the file entry point and brought failure handling and the event exit into the same relationship. That is why the three downstream terms were written in parallel rather than split into three small diagrams. This made the lookup order straightforward: confirm Railtie first, inspect initialization next, then circle back to failure- and event-related content.

That sequence also shaped the wording of the notes. “Initialization” was treated as the next step after Railtie; “failure” was placed after initialization; and “event exit” was placed on the final layer together with failure. The page therefore drew reading targets at different levels of detail as a sequence of steps, assuming that all of them could be found near the entry point.

DOC-08 is a short record of calls adjacent to init. The old reading treated it as the lower half of this diagram: move from Railtie into initialization, then use the area around initialization to branch into the remaining directions. When the two pages are viewed together, they easily create an overly smooth impression, as if the init note had filled in all of Railtie's relationships.

## Later Margin Notes

On review, the value of the diagram as a lookup aid was retained, not the meaning of its arrows. `lib/newrelic_rpm.rb` is still the starting point; Railtie is still worth finding first; and initialization, failure, and event exit are still the locations to distinguish after entering the file. These four items are simply no longer suitable for being represented by one vertical line as a fixed sequence.

“Failure” was originally only a reminder term in the diagram. Once it appeared, readers often went looking for a failure branch immediately following initialization; but the original record neither wrote failure handling as a standalone object nor recorded an adjacency relationship between it and the event exit. “Event exit” worked the same way: it marked a direction that needed further attention, but the layout turned it into Railtie's endpoint.

Railtie itself played two roles in the old diagram. On one hand, it was the object to look for starting from the file entry point; on the other, the diagram showed it as the node through which initialization, failure, and event exit all passed. The first use works for navigation; the second became the old conclusion that this page was repeatedly cited for. The two were not separated in the original.

## When Continuing to Use This Page

Keeping the original diagram can help readers return from the file entry point to the initial reading route: find Railtie first, then inspect the init-adjacent content, failure-related locations, and event-related locations separately. Do not treat the three items below as an established call order, and do not treat DOC-08 as the latter half of this relationship diagram.

The old conclusion remains here: near `lib/newrelic_rpm.rb`, the relationships among Railtie, initialization, failure handling, and the event exit can all be reviewed at once. It explains why the diagram was drawn this way, and why subsequent lookups always started near the entry point. That conclusion was convenient for locating things, but it should no longer be used to judge direct calls between objects.

The work later added in the diagram's margin focused on recording four items separately: where Railtie appears, the content adjacent to initialization, failure-related locations, and event-related locations. This keeps the original entry point while no longer writing the navigation order as a predetermined path.

title: Context fallback interface proposal

versions.body:
# Context Fallback Interface Proposal

First, record the two names separately. Invalid carrier fallback refers to the case where the carrier has arrived, but its traceparent cannot serve as upstream input; Current span fallback refers to the case where the call site has not obtained usable upstream context and may instead inspect the current span. Both are called fallbacks, but their trigger conditions may not be the same.

The current working assumption is that after extraction fails, we can continue checking other sources. This assumption is only for structuring the discussion and should not be used to modify callers. It has an obvious counterexample: before entering the bridge, the caller may already carry a OpenTelemetry::Context. If, after a bad carrier arrives, we immediately start selecting context again, the so-called “fallback” could become an overwrite of existing state.

Therefore, the checks should first be split into three: whether the carrier has a traceparent, whether that value is usable, and whether the call site already had context. List Current span fallback separately; it concerns a candidate with no retrievable upstream context and should not be inferred directly from the invalid case.

The old header should not be the default path yet. It is worth comparing further only if we can show that it will not change state already held by the caller and can distinguish bad input from empty input. Otherwise, retain the existing entry point and do not combine the two issues into one chain.

After review, three items remain unresolved: where the current span is obtained, whether it already exists at the relevant call sites, and whether any existing consumers of the legacy header still require compatibility.

# Context Fallback Interface Proposal

The initial draft from 2023 put Invalid carrier fallback and Current span fallback into a single sequence to give the interface discussion something concrete to compare: when carrier extraction yields no result, try the old header; if there is still no result, check the current span. That passage remains on this page because many later questions came from this shorthand.

On review, combining them became an obstacle in itself. Unusable carrier contents do not mean the call site has no upstream context; having a current span at the call site does not mean it can replace the OpenTelemetry::Context the caller already holds. The old draft's “no result” compressed at least three situations into one phrase: missing carrier contents, unusable contents supplied by the carrier, and no usable upstream state at the call site.

## Separate the Things Being Compared First

A carrier can contain extractable data, be missing data, or contain unusable data. Caller state raises a different question: does context already exist before entering the bridge? The same `fallback` name should not stand in for an answer to both questions.

The early discussion treated traceparent as the only field to check. That record still has value because it shows that the starting point was carrier extraction, not where the current span was obtained. But it was too narrow: even if traceparent is unusable, we still need to know what the caller brought in. If the caller already has context, “finding another source” is not necessarily filling a gap.

The first review raised a direct challenge: why should an unusable carrier be allowed to trigger context replacement? The initial draft did not answer it. It assumed fallback meant recovery, without distinguishing between recovering missing state and overwriting existing state. The draft subsequently added “the caller already has context” to what needed to be examined, but has not yet fully separated it from current span as a candidate source.

## Retained Old Sequence

> When extraction from the carrier fails, try the legacy header; if there is still no result, use the current span directly.

This is no longer a recommendation. It links invalid input, legacy-format compatibility, and current span availability into a result-driven sequence. If the result changes, we cannot tell whether bad input triggered an alternative source or there was no upstream context to begin with, nor can we tell whether the legacy header played a part in the selection.

Withdrawing this sequence does not mean we have proved that the legacy header is invalid everywhere, or that the current span can never be used. What is being withdrawn is only the idea of “automatically continuing along the same chain to find a source when the carrier is unusable.” If the legacy header still has consumers, it should be raised as a separate compatibility issue; if Current span fallback still exists, it should first identify which kind of call with no upstream context it addresses.

## Review of the Old Investigation Starting Point

The old investigation notes pointed to `.github/actions/issue_closer/dist/index.js` through the issue name and call name. In `internal/ruby-agent-core`'s `v_prev`, that path can still serve as a starting point for further inspection of references, but it cannot establish ownership of the bridge implementation on its own.

The early discussion turned “related names can be found near this starting point” into “the old header is accepted here.” We no longer use that conclusion. The proximity of the file location, issue name, and call name only explains why the investigation started here at the time; it does not prove that carrier parsing, legacy header compatibility, and current span selection happen in the same place.

This review also exposed a wording problem. The old draft used “existing context” for both the OpenTelemetry::Context brought in by the caller and the current span observed at runtime. The two may be related, but they are not the same thing to compare. The former is state that existed before the call; the latter is only a candidate source that still needs confirmation. Continuing to use these terms interchangeably would give the impression that the boundaries of Current span fallback have already been established.

## What Still Needs to Be Compared in This Round

| Situation | What to examine first | What not to assume follows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The carrier contains a usable traceparent | How the extracted context connects to subsequent context | Do not bring current span into the discussion as a side issue |
| The carrier lacks extractable contents | Whether the call site already has context | Do not call this bad input |
| The carrier contents are unusable | Whether the existing context is touched | Do not automatically accept the old header |
| There is no upstream context | The source and scope of the current span | Do not infer this from the invalid case |

The fourth row remains unresolved. It does not require always using the current span as the default source. It requires establishing exactly which kind of “no upstream context” the call site faces before retaining this candidate. If the caller already has explicit state, Current span fallback should not become an additional reason to replace it.

This round will not add a general-purpose interface or a compatibility layer for the old header. The material to bring back to review is two verifiable snapshots: whether caller state changes before and after carrier extraction fails, and where the current span is obtained when there is no upstream context. If these two points are not on the same call chain, the proposal should be split into two local decisions.

DOC-16 records the exception boundaries for Span attribute mutation and Segment finish propagation. It can serve as a nearby navigation reference, but provides no conclusions about current span or legacy header for this proposal.

Still undecided: whether the legacy header still has actual consumers; whether Current span fallback covers all existing calls; whether the two types of input should share the same test fixture.

# Context Fallback Interface Proposal

This material was not maintained as a complete interface specification. It originally just grouped together several easily confused names, and later went through review, entry-point verification, and card addenda, so not all of the old paragraphs were removed. Looking back now, Invalid carrier fallback, Current span fallback, legacy header, and caller context referred to different comparison targets at different stages.

When reading old paragraphs, first consider their historical layer. The earlier ordering was only the working assumption at the time; crossed-out paths are not compatibility commitments that were later reconfirmed. The scope currently in use appears later, and only constrains the local relationship between a malformed traceparent and the caller context.

## 2023-06-26: Initial Record

The initial version described the problem as a fallback chain: first extract from the carrier; if extraction failed, try the legacy header; if there was still no result, check the current span. At the time, this ordering had a limited purpose: it gave the interface review a starting point for comparison.

The initial draft treated the traceparent in the carrier as the primary input. The working assumption then was that as long as extraction did not produce a usable result, it could continue looking for another source. This wording was short and easy to remember, but it did not explain whether “no result” meant that the carrier lacked content, that the carrier content was unusable, or that the call site had no upstream context at all.

The initial draft also left one unanswered question: if the caller already had OpenTelemetry::Context before entering the bridge, could source selection still start after a bad carrier arrived? There was not enough local material at the time to answer this, so it only stated that “fallback should not replace existing state without cause.” This was a risk note, not an implemented rule.

In the initial record, Current span fallback was only a candidate. It was placed at the end of the chain, as if it could be used whenever the preceding options produced no result; but the record did not say where the current span came from or whether it existed for all calls. Later discussions started here by distinguishing “the last candidate” from “the existing behavior when there is no upstream context.”

## 2023-06-27: Review Addendum

The review did not accept the generalization that “no result means fallback.” The changes left behind split the comparison into two dimensions: the carrier’s own state and the caller’s state upon entering the call site.

The carrier may have a usable traceparent, lack extractable content, or provide content that cannot be used. The caller, separately, must be checked for whether context already exists. Both questions appear to concern fallback, but they cannot be answered by the same name.

The counterexamples in the review are very concrete: if the caller already has context, why should an invalid carrier be allowed to trigger replacement? The old draft assumed that fallback was “filling in,” but did not distinguish filling in missing state from rewriting existing state. The subsequent draft added “the original state at the entry point” as an observation item.

However, this review did not make a cross-call decision about Current span fallback. Some people leaned toward retaining it first and then splitting out the old header; others believed that, without facts about the call site, neither should be the default. In the end, the only agreement was that subsequent checks must state both whether the carrier is valid and whether the caller already had context. This agreement is clearer than the old ordering, but it is still not an interface commitment.

## Original text of the early proposal, retained for identification

> When the carrier cannot be extracted, try the legacy header; if there is still no result, use the current span directly.

**This passage is deprecated.** It once helped list the entry points in one place, but it must not be used to guide changes now. The issue is not that it has been proven that the old header is always unusable, nor that the current span can never be used; the issue is that it compressed three matters requiring separate confirmation into one sequence: the carrier input state, whether the caller already has context, and whether the legacy header remains an independent compatibility entry point.

The old ordering also has a troubleshooting defect. When the result changes, this chain alone cannot determine whether bad input triggered an alternative source, whether the call site originally had no upstream context, or whether the old header participated in the selection. A single result may appear to support multiple explanations, making it impossible to clarify the behavioral boundaries.

Therefore, going forward, “what was ultimately obtained” will no longer be treated as the sole criterion. First ask what the caller originally had at the entry point; only after confirming that there is no usable upstream context is Current span fallback a candidate requiring separate verification. If the legacy header does have actual adopters, it must also be documented separately from the adoption point, rather than being introduced automatically because the carrier is invalid.

## 2024-04-29: Corrections left by the entry-point review

The old investigation record pointed from the issue name and call name to `.github/actions/issue_closer/dist/index.js`. This path is retained as historical navigation: in the `v_prev` of `internal/ruby-agent-core`, when reconstructing why the old investigation started from this name, you can continue by following the reference relationships in that file.

However, the early record had written “a related name can be found near the entry point” as “the old header will be accepted here.” This sentence was later explicitly crossed out. The proximity of the file location, issue name, and call name can only indicate the starting point of the search at that time; it cannot prove that carrier parsing, legacy header compatibility, and current span selection occurred in the same place, nor can it replace a review of the actual call relationships.

This review also corrected another term. In the old draft, “existing context” sometimes referred to the OpenTelemetry::Context supplied by the caller, and sometimes to the current span visible at runtime. The two may be related, but they are not the same object. The former is state that already exists before the call; the latter is only a candidate source yet to be confirmed. Referring to both as “existing context” would make it look as though the review had already verified the scope of Current span fallback, when in fact it had not.

The comparison table retained at the time is below. It is not the current rule table; its purpose was to prevent the review from folding several questions back into the same branch again.

| Scenario | What had to be checked first at the time | What could not be assumed at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| carrier has a usable traceparent | How the extracted context connects | Do not also discuss current span |
| carrier has no extractable content | Whether context already exists at the call site | Do not call it bad input |
| carrier content is unusable | Whether the original state is touched | Do not automatically try the old header |
| No upstream context | Where current span is obtained | Do not infer this from the invalid case |

The fourth row had no conclusion at the time, and the historical table cannot supply one now. It only fixed the order of comparison: first confirm whether there really is no upstream context, then ask whether current span is an existing choice or a runtime object that happens to be visible.

## An unfinished review record

During the review, there was a plan to compare two kinds of observations side by side: one was whether the caller's state changed before and after carrier extraction failed; the other was where current span was obtained when there was no upstream context. That plan did not thereby become a global experimental conclusion. The only takeaway that can be retained is that, if the two are not in the same call chain, they should not be forced into a single change merely for terminological consistency.

A more radical approach was also proposed at the time: simply remove Current span fallback from the discussion as well, leaving only carrier extraction. This approach was not adopted. The reason was not that current span had already been proven necessary to retain, but that there was no evidence showing that all existing calls did not need it. Treating usage sites that had not been found as nonexistent would repeat the early misreading of “inferring the entire behavior from a single entry point.”

Another unfinished item was legacy header. The old chain described it as a second source after invalid, but the review did not confirm whether it still had any specific consumers. It therefore could neither remain a default compensating fallback nor be declared removed without any identified usage sites. This question remained on this page rather than being packaged as a compatibility strategy that had already been finalized.

## 2025-09: Boundaries brought back by the risk review

OTEL-202 included Invalid carrier fallback in the risk review, and it was subsequently taken up for handling. The card retains `OpenTelemetry::Context` and `traceparent` as search terms. These correspond exactly to the two layers that had previously been conflated: the former is the caller's state, and the latter is the input in the carrier.

This card is not a complete design decision. It does not establish how all carrier forms should be handled, nor does it provide a basis for adopting legacy header. What it brings back is a local constraint: when discussing a bad carrier, we cannot look only at the traceparent parsing result; we must also consider the caller's existing context.

This material makes the early approach of “checking only traceparent” insufficient, but there is no need to turn it into a generalized rule in the opposite direction. A carrier lacking content and a carrier providing unusable content still need to be distinguished; whether upstream context exists also remains a separate question.

## 2025-10：Supplementary note on Current span

The baseline record for OTEL-218 retains the observation that “the existing call retains Current span fallback”. A subsequent supplementary note points out that one aspect of this fallback remains unconfirmed and needs further checking through the same entry point. Here, the supplementary note is not extended into a judgment about all calls.

The value of this record is that it prevents another overgeneralization. The fact that one existing call retains Current span fallback does not imply that an invalid carrier should also lead to current span. The former describes a candidate in an existing call; the latter concerns whether the caller's state may be changed when the carrier input is unusable. Both terms contain fallback, but they do not share the same premise.

At this point, the comparison criteria for the proposal have stabilized: for a bad carrier, check whether the caller's existing state is overwritten; only for calls without upstream context should we continue verifying where current span is obtained and its scope. legacy header remains a separate compatibility issue, unless a new, specific call relationship connects it to a particular branch.

## Review record：Choosing between two candidates

The retained review notes frame the choice as two candidates, rather than continuing to modify the old fallback chain.

- Candidate A：Handle invalid carrier and the absence of upstream context together, with both proceeding to a lookup of legacy header or current span.
- Candidate B：For invalid carrier, handle only the input failure itself; discuss Current span fallback only under the separate condition that there is no upstream context.

Candidate A has the advantage of a short sequence and is also consistent with the earliest records. Its problem is that there is no clear protection point when the caller already holds a OpenTelemetry::Context; once a result is disputed, the records also make it difficult to show which layer actually made the choice.

Candidate B adds a branch and appears more verbose during review, but it separates bad input from missing state. If legacy header compatibility is needed, it can only be discussed as an independent source, rather than being included automatically because the carrier is unavailable. Subsequent verification follows Candidate B's distinction.

The review did not draw a cross-call conclusion about Current span fallback. The available material supports only two local facts: “existing calls retain it” and “one other location still needs to be checked.” Describing it as the default for all calls, or as already completely removed, would go beyond what the records support.

## Scope of the currently adopted handling

The current approach addresses only the local boundary of Invalid carrier fallback: when the traceparent in the carrier is unusable, that event is not treated as a reason to reselect the caller's context.

Invalid traceparent input leaves the caller's OpenTelemetry::Context unchanged instead of invoking legacy header acceptance.

This requirement is limited to invalid traceparent input, applies specifically to the caller's OpenTelemetry::Context, and also specifies that legacy header acceptance is not used. It does not say that the context remains unchanged whenever any carrier is missing, nor does it add or remove a general rule for Current span fallback.

This scope was adopted to address the counterexample raised at the outset: bad input cannot serve as a basis for overwriting the caller's existing state. It also avoids disguising the historical compatibility issue with legacy headers as default recovery after a parsing failure. If legacy header calls that still need support are confirmed later, a compatibility approach should be proposed again based on the specific point of use, with an explanation of how that entry point relates to invalid traceparent; the shorthand for the old fallback chain must not be reinstated.

The conditions for reopening this comparison should also remain local. The comparison should be reopened only if subsequent verification finds that the caller's context is not the state that this entry point needs to preserve, or confirms that legacy headers must be accepted in invalid traceparent cases without changing that state. At that point, the actual call relationships need to be supplied; “there is still fallback” alone cannot be used to return to the old judgment.

## Adjacent issues that have not disappeared with this decision

Current span fallback did not disappear because of this decision. The existing calls recorded by OTEL-218 remain concrete clues, and one of them is still unconfirmed. For now, the question can only be stated as: under the call condition where no upstream context is available, is current span a retained existing choice, or merely a runtime object that happens to exist? The conclusion about Invalid carrier does not answer this question.

When checking Current span fallback, invalid carrier should not be treated as a prerequisite. First confirm whether the call site has usable upstream context; if not, then confirm where current span is obtained and whether it falls within the expected scope of that call. If these two checks fall on different call chains, record them separately.

DOC-16 handles edge cases involving Span attribute mutation and Segment finish propagation. It concerns the same bridge-adjacent area as this discussion, but does not provide a conclusion about Current span fallback; navigate there when reviewing adjacent impacts, but do not bring finish semantics back into this proposal.

It has not yet been confirmed on this page whether legacy header still has any adopters that must be retained. Earlier text placed it in the invalid branch because it did not first distinguish the input state; this cannot now be used as the basis for retaining or removing compatibility behavior. If someone confirms a specific adoption point, a subsequent proposal should explain the relationship between the input it receives and caller's OpenTelemetry::Context.

## Appendix of Legacy Examples

### Legacy Example A: Conflating missing and unavailable into “no traceparent”

The old example only asked whether the carrier provided traceparent. Not providing it and providing it but having it be unusable then both entered the same fallback description. This example no longer applies because it cannot express what should happen when caller already has OpenTelemetry::Context. It remains here to help identify the same wording in old tests and old discussions.

### Legacy Example B: Treating current span as the final fallback layer

The old example described current span as the final layer, as if it could be used whenever preceding sources returned no result. This example is also outdated. It omitted the prerequisite of “no upstream context” and obscured the fact that Current span fallback still has an unconfirmed location. Going forward, when the same wording appears, first determine whether it describes the old ordering or a call condition that has already been independently confirmed.

### Legacy Example C: Inferring compatibility behavior from the entry file

The earlier investigation started from `.github/actions/issue_closer/dist/index.js` and mistakenly treated the ability to find related names as evidence of behavior. That path is now retained only for historical navigation. It explains why this file appears on this page, but no longer serves as a basis for judgments about legacy header, carrier parsing, or current span selection.

## Check sequence retained at the end of the page

For subsequent changes, first confirm which type of trigger is involved: an unusable traceparent in the carrier, a carrier with no extractable content, or a call site with no upstream context. Only the first type falls directly under this page's current requirements. The second and third types must not be assigned the invalid conclusion merely because their names are similar.

For the first type, checks before and after should focus on the caller's existing OpenTelemetry::Context. Only for the third type should local verification of Current span fallback begin. The legacy header remains a separate compatibility issue until new facts about calls explicitly connect it to a particular branch.

The reason for retaining the historical material this way is not to maintain the old claims, but to ensure that each judgment still has an identifiable place: the original unified fallback chain has been abandoned; the review separated input from state; the entry-point recheck corrected the misreading that inferred behavior from file location; the two cards separately restored local clues about invalid and current span; the current requirements focus only on the impact of invalid traceparent on the caller's context. The remaining unconfirmed points are still retained, pending specific call relationships before they are split further.

# Span Attribute and Finish Propagation Troubleshooting Tree

First separate the two things that are often conflated in incident notes: whether custom attributes are still on the Span after the attribute call, and whether attributes that were previously visible can still be seen after Segment finish. Both may be described as “gone after finish,” but the time the issue is discovered cannot stand in for the time when the change occurred.

The old record points to `lib/new_relic/agent.rb`. Start here to confirm whether the record at hand concerns the attribute call or the object around finish; no complete call relationship was recorded at the time, so do not assign the issue to a particular piece of finish logic based only on this entry point.

For attribute anomalies, check in this order:

- No target custom attribute before the call: leave it in the caller-side incident record.
- Not visible immediately after the call: record it as an observation of Span attribute mutation; do not continue explaining it through the finish process.
- Visible after the call but not after finish: add an observation from before finish; without this step, the sample cannot be written up as Segment finish propagation.

During on-call investigation, keep the attribute name and value the same. Do not change the attribute name, value, failure condition, and finish timing in the same sample; even if the attribute is ultimately not visible, that makes it impossible to compare where the first change occurred.

The old rule of thumb was “if the attribute is missing after finish, check finish first.” It remains here as a starting point, but it was only a quick guess at the time. If the attribute was already not visible after the call, its subsequent absence after finish adds no new information.

To fill in: whether the attribute can be observed before finish under failure conditions; and how many old samples recorded only the single post-finish result.

# Span Attributes and Finish Propagation Troubleshooting Tree

This page still starts from two observation points: after Span attribute mutation, whether the custom attributes remain; and after Segment finish, whether what was originally visible in the observed state has changed. They often show up in the same result, but they shouldn't be explained by the same hypothesis.

## Original Branching

The original entry point is `lib/new_relic/agent.rb`. The old troubleshooting record retained only the issue name, call name, and this path. Someone followed the filename and attributed the missing attributes directly to finish, reasoning, “It was only noticed after finish.” That reasoning only shows that the discovery happened after finish; it does not show that the change happened during the finish action.

The original manual tree is retained as follows:

```text
Attribute not visible
├─ No custom attribute before the call
│  └─ Inspect the caller
├─ Not visible immediately after the call
│  └─ Inspect the attribute mutation
└─ Visible after the call, not visible after finish
   └─ Inspect the finish path
```

The last branch itself is not a problem; the problem is that the confirmation that it was “visible after the call” was often skipped. Without that observation, we cannot say the case has reached the last branch.

## On-Call Note

During troubleshooting, hold one attribute name and one attribute value fixed. If the attribute name, value, exception behavior, and finish timing all change at once, the result is a sequence that cannot be compared. All the case needs to retain is a few brief observations: after the attribute call, before finish, and after finish—whether the same key is still visible.

If there was no custom attribute before the call, don't inspect finish just to complete the flow. If the attribute is already gone after the call, don't treat the post-finish behavior as new evidence. Both branches should stop locally and keep the sample at their respective observation points.

Someone once described “the attribute is still on the Span” and “the attribute has already propagated to the Segment side” as the same thing. That wording should no longer be used. The former is a local observation after the call; the latter requires at least a before-and-after-finish comparison.

## Review Addendum

The review did not confirm the original judgment that “visible before finish necessarily means it will be carried through with finish.” The original sentence was not deleted because old issues will still use similar wording; it is no longer a routing rule.

The safer order is:

1. State which custom attribute this observation covers; don't use the generic term “attributes”.
2. Check once after the attribute call; if it is already missing here, stop at Span attribute mutation.
3. If the attribute is still present, check again before finish to rule out changes in between.
4. Only when it is visible before finish and not visible after finish should the observation be recorded under Segment finish propagation.

Here, “stop” means stop attributing the cause, not stop preserving the evidence. When it is not visible after the call, still record the attribute name, value, and post-call result; just don't continue along the finish path looking for a plausible-sounding explanation.

## Unresolved Attempt

Someone once suggested treating missing attributes during an exception and missing attributes during normal finish as one issue. This suggestion did not produce a usable conclusion. An exception changes the observation order, while normal finish may not pass through the same visibility states; once the two types of samples are put in the same bucket, it becomes impossible to tell what is being compared.

At present, the normal path and the exception-related path are marked separately. When a stable pre-finish observation is unavailable in the exception case, don't use the normal-path conclusion to fill the gap; preserve only the state that was actually visible.

## Deprecated Short Conclusion

> “If an attribute is missing after Segment finish, start investigating from finish.”

This sentence no longer applies. It can remain as a search term for old records, but it cannot continue to serve as the handling order. The actual routing depends on the observation point at which the same attribute first stops being visible.

```text
Custom attribute anomaly observed
|
+-- Not retained after the attribute call
|   `-- Retain the post-call result; stop at attribute mutation
|
+-- Retained after the attribute call, disappears before finish
|   `-- Retain the intermediate observation; don't attribute it directly to finish
|
+-- Retained before finish, disappears after finish
|   `-- Record it as a finish propagation observation
|
`-- No comparable observations
    `-- Add samples only; don't fill in the cause
```

The third branch should say “retained before finish, disappears after finish”; don't shorten it to “finish loses attribute”. The former preserves the basis for the judgment; the latter mistakes the discovery point for the point of change.

To fill in: whether a pre-finish observation can always be obtained in the exception path; among the samples called “finish propagation” in old records, how many actually had only a single post-finish check.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Span Attributes and Finish Propagation

This page started as old notes dug up for shift scheduling. The first things preserved were not a complete design description, but a file path, a few brief notes saying “attributes disappeared,” and the phrase “only noticed after finishing.” Several later rounds of cleanup left these original words intact, because the same wording still turns up in old issues; if only the later, corrected tree remained, readers would have trouble seeing why the early investigation went astray.

We still start from `lib/new_relic/agent.rb`. This path appears repeatedly in the old notes because both the original issue name and the call name pointed to it. It is useful for confirming the scope of what you are reading: are you looking at the area around a Span attribute call, or the area around a Segment finish? It is not proof of where the implementation belongs. The early material did not preserve enough call relationships to infer from the entry file that any particular object is responsible for clearing, copying, or retaining attributes.

When investigating, do not rush to label something as “lost.” Choose one custom attribute and record whether the same key is visible after the attribute call, before finishing, and after finishing. The observation points are only meaningful if the item being compared stays the same. If you change the attribute name, value, exception conditions, and finish timing all in one sample, you can usually only see the final difference afterward, without being able to say where it first appeared.

---

## Original Passage Left in 6 of 2023

The initial rule was brief: if an attribute is not visible after finishing, check Segment finish first. This rule came from the order in which things were discovered at the time, not from confirmation of the internal state. It turned “I saw the problem after finishing” into “the problem must have been caused by finishing.”

The original draft contained a small tree, preserved here:

```text
Attribute not visible
├─ No custom attribute even before the call
│  └─ Check the caller
├─ Not visible immediately after the call
│  └─ Check attribute changes
└─ Visible after the call, not visible after finishing
   └─ Check the finish path
```

The person on duty at the time would usually jump straight to the last branch. User reports often provided only the result after the transaction or Segment had already finished, and the most prominent word was finish. But the last branch has prerequisites: the attribute was visible after the attribute call, and it was still visible before finishing. Without these two intermediate observations, the last branch is just a convenient guess.

This passage has not been deleted because old issues and verbal handoffs still say “finish loses attributes.” When you encounter this phrase, first return to its original meaning: it describes where the problem was noticed, not a confirmed point where the change occurred. If an old sample contains only a single result from after finishing, keep its original classification, but note alongside it that comparisons after the call and before finishing are missing.

## A Note Beside the Early Shift Notes

Someone later wrote a sentence beside the original tree: do not substitute “whether the finish method was entered” for observing the attribute. Reaching a nearby point only shows that the program got there; it does not show that the custom attribute changed there.

The minimum record agreed on at the time was not a complete log, but three short lines:

- After the attribute call: whether the attribute name and value are visible;
- Before Segment finish: whether the same attribute name and value are visible;
- After Segment finish: whether the same attribute name and value are visible.

If the first row is already empty, stop on the attribute mutation side. If the first row has it but the second row is empty, finish is not the only candidate; the intermediate state has already changed first. Only when it is visible in both of the first two rows but not in the third should the sample be placed on the finish propagation side.

This addition was once interpreted as requiring three complete screenshots every time. That is not the case. The focus is on comparing several points in time, not on the screenshot format. If a particular point in time cannot be observed, simply record the gap; do not fabricate “what it should look like.” Likewise, if the attribute key is still present but its value has changed, this cannot simply be called a loss. This page deals with the visibility boundaries of keys, not with explaining whether a business action updated a value.

## The old quick procedure, no longer recommended

Below are the short steps originally circulated in 2023:

1. Observe that the attribute is missing after finish.
2. Look for the finish call near `lib/new_relic/agent.rb`.
3. If you see attribute-related objects, describe the issue as finish propagation.

This section is outdated. The second step can still serve as a starting point for reading, but the third step is not valid. Objects near the file, a single call, and a single observation from the actual case are not the same kind of evidence. The old steps saved time then, but also missed samples where “the attribute was already absent after the attribute call.”

If an old issue contains only the sentence “it was gone after finish,” do not retroactively record it as a finish propagation anomaly. You can retain its old classification and add “observations after the call and before finish were not recorded.” This neither rewrites the original situation nor lets later readers mistake the classification for a conclusion.

---

## Review in 2024, month 4: find the first change first

During the second round of organizing the material, the review focus shifted from “what happened at finish” to “at which observation point the same attribute first became invisible.” This was a small change, but in practice it split the troubleshooting tree into separate branches.

```text
Attribute anomaly found
|
+-- No attribute before the call
|   `-- Outside this page's scope of judgment; retain the caller's observation
|
+-- No attribute after the call
|   `-- Record as an observation of Span attribute mutation, then stop
|
+-- Present after the call, absent before finish
|   `-- Retain the intermediate observation; cannot attribute directly to finish
|
+-- Present before finish, absent after finish
|   `-- Proceed to the Segment finish propagation record
|
`-- Intermediate observation points missing
    `-- Add samples only; do not fill in a cause
```

Here, “stop” means stop attributing a cause, not stop saving evidence. When the attribute is not visible after the call, the attribute name, value, and result after the call should still be retained; just do not continue along the finish path looking for a story that could explain it. The same applies when it is already invisible before finish: finish may still be part of the same flow, but the existing samples are insufficient to place the change at the finish action.

The review also left behind an uncomfortable fact: samples previously written up as “attribute retention” did not necessarily all observe custom attributes. Some records only show that the Span still exists, or that other fields remain visible. The existence of a Span and the continued presence of a particular custom attribute are not the same determination. New records should name the specific attribute instead of using “attributes are fine” as a substitute.

## The Failed Attempt That Was Kept

At the time, there was an attempt to combine normal termination and abnormal termination into a single comparison. This attempt was not carried through, not because it had been proven wrong, but because the observation order for the two types of samples was different. In an abnormal case, the exception may be observed first, followed by an attempt to finish; a normal case has no such interruption point. Once the two types of samples were placed into “before finish/after finish” columns, the column names were the same, but the actual points in time were not necessarily the same.

A very thin table from the failed attempt still remains:

| Sample | Last confirmed visible point | Missing observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal termination | After the attribute call or before termination | The result after termination may be missing |
| Exception-related incident | When the exception was observed | Whether it passed through the same point adjacent to termination |

This table does not provide causal attribution. It only reminds investigators: an exceptional path cannot borrow the term “before termination” from the normal path unless the same point in time was actually observed. The part of the old page that collectively referred to exceptional samples as “lost after finish” no longer applies.

## A Counterquestion Left by One Review

During the review, someone asked: if everything is ultimately seen after termination, why distinguish these points in time? At the time, the answer was not written up as a design conclusion; only two counterexamples were left.

The first counterexample is that the attribute becomes immediately invisible after the attribute call. Regardless of whether the Segment subsequently finishes, the missing attribute seen after termination is the same state that had already occurred. The second counterexample is that the attribute is visible after the attribute call but not visible before termination. In that case, its remaining invisible after termination adds no new information. Only after excluding these two counterexamples can the before-and-after-termination observations be said to show a change.

This counterquestion is more useful to consult during on-call duty than the old rule because it does not require first believing some implementation detail. It only requires separating the point when something was discovered from the point when it changed. Therefore, when seeing a description such as “no attribute after termination,” first ask whether the record contains the result after the call, and then ask whether it contains the result before termination; do not first choose a cause from the wording.

---

## An Old Misreading of the Entry File

`lib/new_relic/agent.rb` was cited so often that some people treated it as the place where every answer should ultimately land. One reading record amplified this misreading: as long as Span or the text API was seen near the file, the incident was classified as an attribute change; as long as finish-related words were seen, the incident was classified as propagation.

The later correction was not to replace one filename with another, but to restore the order of the objects. First inspect the object actually called in the sample, then inspect that object's attributes after the call; only if necessary should you inspect the period before and after termination. The entry file provides only nearby navigation and cannot replace the object relationships in the sample.

Therefore, the following wording should no longer be added:

- “The path contains termination logic, so termination clears the attributes.”
- “The Span is still there, so the custom attributes are too.”
- “The exception appears here, so it follows the same branch as normal termination.”

They all compress observations from different layers into a single sentence. Similar sentences that already appear in old records do not need to be uniformly removed, but new records must no longer use this kind of sentence in place of a sample.

## Minimal sampling that still applies

For a specific sample, first choose a custom attribute that will not be renamed during the process. When recording it, do not list the entire attribute set; when the set is too large, the person making the comparison can often only confirm that “it looks different” and cannot determine whether the same key exists. It is sufficient to save the state of that key at several observation points.

If the value itself changes as a result of business actions, do not directly call differing values missing. For a sample where the value changes but the key remains visible, write “key visible, value changed”; do not put it into Segment finish propagation. If the key name exists but the value is empty, do not automatically classify it as missing. The old material did not establish a rule that “an empty value equals removal”; here, you can only write “key visible, value empty” and then stop.

This limitation also applies to records where only the final state is visible. A normal final state does not mean that the state was normal after the call, before finish, and after finish; an abnormal final state does not mean that the change necessarily occurred at finish. In the past, some records filled in unobserved samples as “no anomaly” to make it easier to close out the incident. That practice is no longer used. Unobserved means unobserved; it can be backfilled later or left blank indefinitely.

---

## Samples reopened in the 2025 year

During reorganization, OTEL-203 was retained as field navigation. The card requires the visible result of Span attribute mutation in one successful call and one failed call to be recorded separately. This requirement does not provide a code-level attribution for this page, but it adds a comparison method that is often missing from old records: the same attribute should be observed separately in the successful and failed cases; do not save only the final result from the failed side.

“Successful call” and “failed call” are sample labels here. They do not guarantee that the two samples went through the same finish process, and they do not guarantee that a single comparison can identify the cause. They can only help confirm at which observation point a particular attribute first begins to differ; they cannot be used to skip the intermediate observations.

If the successful sample records only the after-finish state, while the failed sample records the states after the call, before finish, and after finish, the two still cannot establish a difference in finish propagation. The reverse is also true. When the samples are asymmetric, first fill in the side with less information rather than inferring the other side from the more complete one.

OTEL-203 underwent one rollback verification and was then processed again. This action shows that the previous closeout was not enough to make the issue disappear, but it provides no new code-level conclusion. The old page must not write “processing restarted” as “the finish path has been confirmed to be incorrect.” Rollback verification and restarting are both field states, not proof of the attribute implementation.

## Current triage wording

Only from this point onward does the current requirement apply. For samples clearly within the scope of Span attribute calls, **Span#set_attribute and Span#add_attributes remain available and preserve custom span attributes.** This statement addresses only the availability of attribute API and the preservation of custom Span attributes; it does not assign any specific implementation attribution to Segment finish propagation.

Therefore, when an attribute anomaly is observed, record it in the following order:

```text
Start: Select a custom span attribute
|
+-- Not visible after the attribute call
|   |
|   +-- Record the call and the result for that attribute
|   +-- Classify as: Span attribute mutation
|   `-- Stop; do not reclassify it as finish propagation
|
+-- Visible after the attribute call
    |
    +-- Not visible before finish
    |   |
    |   +-- Record the observation between the last visible point and the first invisible point
    |   `-- Do not yet place the change on Segment finish
    |
    +-- Visible before finish
        |
        +-- Not visible after finish
        |   `-- Classify as: Segment finish propagation
        |
        +-- Still visible after finish
        |   `-- No anomaly on this page; do not open an additional propagation issue
        |
        `-- Not observed after finish
            `-- Retain the incomplete sample; do not add a conclusion
```

This tree places “attribute API is still available” and “the observed behavior after a particular finish” in different positions. The former is not a shortcut to the latter. Even if the attribute is briefly visible after the call, there must still be a comparison from before to after finish before the sample can be written to the propagation branch; even if it is not visible after finish, that cannot be used in turn to deny the availability of the attribute call itself.

For on-call records, not being visible after the attribute call is an explicit stopping point. Continuing to trace Segment finish only repeats the recording of the same subsequently invisible state. Being already invisible before finish is also a stopping point: it can confirm that the change occurred before the post-finish check, but cannot, based on that alone, determine which intermediate object it occurred in. If no result was obtained after finish, that is neither “still visible” nor “propagation failed”; retain the unobserved state, and do not fill in an answer just to make the tree reach a leaf.

When an anomaly interrupts observation, the sequence may differ from that of a normal sample. Record only the observation points actually obtained; do not copy the normal sample's timeline to the anomalous sample. If the pre-finish observation cannot be obtained on the anomaly path, the tree can only stop at “not compared”; do not attribute the blank to either attribute API or finish propagation.

## Old judgments still being referenced

> If there is a custom attribute, it should be carried over to the Segment side when finishing.

This sentence remains in the middle of the old page and should no longer be treated as a premise for current operations. It combines “whether the attribute is retained,” “when finishing happens,” and “whether it can be seen somewhere after finishing” into a single judgment. The current triage first confirms the state after the attribute call, then determines whether samples from before and after finishing are needed.

> If the attribute cannot be seen after finishing, that means the finish path overwrote it.

This sentence has also been disproven by subsequent observations. Discovering something only after finishing does not mean it changed during finishing. Any old issue that quotes this sentence should have a “first change location not recorded” marker added, rather than having the original sentence quietly rewritten into a correct version.

Keeping these two sentences is not meant to continue endorsing them. People on call will still use similar language to describe what they are seeing. Being able to see the relationship between the original wording and the correction makes it easier to avoid repeating the mistake than leaving only the final tree.

## Review Excerpts Organized

The focus of one review was not which term sounded more natural, but whether the records could be verified. The points compiled are as follows:

- “The attribute exists” must specify which custom attribute is meant; it cannot merely mean that the Span object still exists.
- “Before finishing” must be an actual observation point, not something inferred from reading the code or from convention.
- “Propagation” is used only for samples where the attribute is visible before finishing and not visible afterward; in other cases, record observations, not propagation.
- The entry path helps when revisiting local declarations, but does not replace samples from the incident.

The review did not confirm that the exception path and the normal path share the same implementation, nor did it require rerunning every historical sample. Old samples only need to retain the information they had at the time. New samples should be recorded according to the current tree, to avoid once again treating the final state as the location of the change.

## Using Successful and Failed Samples

Successful and failed calls should each have observations for the same attribute key. They provide a basis for comparison: is the failed sample already different immediately after the call, or does it only become different later? The comparison is not intended to prove that all successful calls represent the same internal path.

Some old records describe “success” as “looking normal in the end.” This wording is insufficient to support comparisons across multiple points in time, but it can still be retained as an old observation. Do not upgrade it to “normal after the call, before finishing, and after finishing.” Likewise, if a failed sample only records that the attribute is missing after finishing, it cannot be upgraded to finish propagation; it is simply a sample awaiting comparison.

## Adjacent Questions Left Open for Now

An adjacent question that has not yet been separated out is: after an exception is observed, can the attribute's last visible state always be obtained at the same location? This question is adjacent to Segment finish propagation, but is not synonymous with it. If an observation before finishing cannot be obtained on the exception path, the record should stop at not compared.

Span link chaining and Exception forwarding are not covered here. They may occur during the same incident, but the sample columns on this page record only custom attributes and their observation points. If links, exception forwarding, and attribute results are written on one line, it will later be difficult to tell which object was actually compared.

## A Short Format for On-Call Records

There is no need for a lengthy narrative. The following format is enough for the next review to know how far the tree was followed:

```text
Attribute key: <actual key name>
After the call: visible / not visible / not observed
Before completion: visible / not visible / not observed
After completion: visible / not visible / not observed
Triage: mutation / propagation / not compared
Notes: exception paths, value changes, or other actual conditions
```

Fill in the content inside angle brackets on site; do not treat the words in the template as results. If the attribute key involves a business name, it may also be kept only in restricted on-site records; this page needs the comparison points, not business data.

“mutation” and “propagation” are troubleshooting triage labels here, not final technical attributions. The former means that the observation after the attribute call is already abnormal; the latter means that the comparison of visible before completion and not visible after completion has been established. Any more specific cause requires additional material and cannot be inferred from the label itself.

---

## Old appendix: On-call transcript from 2023

The following content retains its original level of brevity to make the wording in old issues easier to recognize.

```text
Q: The attribute is not visible after completion.
A: Check agent.rb first; it may be finish.
```

This reply is no longer suitable as an operational procedure. It did not ask whether the attribute was visible after the attribute call, nor whether it was visible before completion. Its only remaining value is to remind readers that the issue at the time left only a single observation result from after completion.

Another old transcript says:

```text
The Span exists, so the attribute should exist too; if you cannot find it, wait for completion to return.
```

This is also outdated. The existence of a Span object cannot replace observation of custom attributes; waiting for completion also cannot make up for the fact that no observations were recorded after the call or before completion. It is retained to explain why the same attribute key and multiple observation points were later included in the on-call format.

## Old appendix: Handling incomplete samples

In the past, unobserved samples were occasionally marked as “no anomalies” to close out an on-site investigation. This practice is no longer used. Not observed means not observed; it can be filled in when subsequent samples become available, or it can remain blank indefinitely. For these records, the most valuable information is usually which observation point is missing, rather than a seemingly complete classification.

If only the result after completion remains, the old page allows it to be marked as “pending comparison”. Do not upgrade it to Segment finish propagation, and do not change it to normal just because the attribute API is currently still available. The two judgments rely on different material.

This page is still referenced by old links, so the old tree, old conclusions, and appendices have not been deleted in their entirety. Actual handling starts with “Current triage format”; when reading historical terminology or early classifications, first check whether they include observations after the call and before completion.

# Invalid Payload and Root Span Decision

The draft placed Invalid trace payload sentinel and Root span parent context on the same transaction thread. That was not because a complete implementation chain already existed, but because the old investigation repeatedly started from `lib/new_relic/agent/transaction.rb`, and trace, payload, sampled, nil, and timestamp could also be found nearby in the file. At the time, the draft chose not to split them into another layer, assuming the two names could temporarily be retained as one batch of context issues.

After review, this judgment needs to be narrowed. A shared reading entry point still exists, but the objects to be verified identified by the two later cards are not the same. Treating identical paths as identical problems saves a record but loses each one's unresolved gap.

## The Draft's Framing

The draft's work sequence was: first examine the result that an invalid payload might leave behind, then examine whether the root span consequently lacks a suitable parent. This sequence came from intuition while reading the file. It listed neither specific callers nor actual versions; at the time, there was also no publicly available sample connecting the two ends.

The original text included this sentence:

> When the payload is unavailable, the root span may not have a suitable parent; investigate them as the same location first.

This sentence will not be removed for now. It explains why the early investigation put the two terms together. The problem is that “might” was later retold as “the same location,” and “the same location” was then understood as the same implementation issue. The draft did not have enough material to support the latter two meanings.

## The Branch Introduced by OTEL-206

The creation note for OTEL-206 was that a legacy call retained the Invalid trace payload result. The card requires checking the callers still using “Invalid trace payload sentinel,” the actual versions, the entry point, and the current result.

This changes how the sentinel branch is recorded. The card focuses on whether legacy calls still use that result, not on whether the word payload appears in the transaction file. The path can help with a lookup, but it cannot replace the caller and version.

After the capacity check, OTEL-206 began processing. The public record leaves only a very narrow indication: one instance of Invalid trace payload sentinel remains unconfirmed. The location of that instance cannot be filled in here, nor can it be written up as a test that has already failed. The only known fact is that the unconfirmed item remains.

If the draft continued placing the sentinel back into “the same batch of transaction issues,” this unconfirmed item could easily be obscured by progress on the root parent. Therefore, this version lists the sentinel separately as a legacy-call verification item.

## The Distinct Gaps in OTEL-222

The creation note for OTEL-222 was that a legacy call retained the Root span parent result. The objects it requires checking also include the caller, actual version, entry point, and current result. The wording is similar to OTEL-206, but similarity does not mean the two cards point to the same call site.

OTEL-222 later began processing, then became blocked while waiting for upstream to provide a publicly available sample. This blockage indicates that review material was missing at the time; it does not indicate where the root span's parent comes from, nor does it indicate that the local path is already problem-free.

Someone suggested early on that the two cards should both be written as “waiting for a sample.” We did not adopt this wording. What is known for OTEL-206 is that one instance remains unconfirmed; what is known for OTEL-222 is that the public sample has not arrived. One means that the item to be verified has not been pinned down; the other means that review material is missing. Collapsing them into one status would leave subsequent readers unable to tell which branch the progress belongs to.

## Reconsidering the Three Approaches

**Approach One: Use the sentinel as the overarching entry point.**

This is the shortest version: first treat Invalid trace payload sentinel as an upstream result, then treat Root span parent context as its downstream manifestation. Not adopted. The existing material does not establish a relationship in which an invalid payload necessarily determines the root parent; filing it this way first would turn an unverified causal relationship into an established fact.

**Approach Two: Use the root parent as the overarching entry point.**

This reverses the relationship and treats the sentinel as a marker for when the parent cannot be obtained. Not adopted either. The root span's legacy result must first be traced to its own caller and entry point; it cannot become the main thread merely because both names contain trace.

**Approach Three: Share the lookup location while keeping the gaps separate.**

This retains repeated review. Both the sentinel and the root parent can start from `lib/new_relic/agent/transaction.rb`, but each record tracks its caller, version, entry point, and result separately. This approach does not provide a compatibility answer, but it does not use one card's material to close out the other card.

This version decides to adopt the third approach.

## Decision in This Version

1. Invalid trace payload sentinel is retained as a legacy-call verification item under OTEL-206; “one instance remains unconfirmed” must not be rewritten as located or cleaned up.
2. Root span parent context is retained as a legacy-call verification item under OTEL-222; waiting for a publicly available sample describes only the blockage at that time and does not indicate the source of the parent.
3. `lib/new_relic/agent/transaction.rb` can serve as the shared lookup location for the two records, but this does not establish a common caller.
4. The draft's phrase “the same batch of legacy context issues” is no longer used as the basis for the decision; it is retained as a record of the early reading habit.

This record still retains traces of the draft's merger because it explains why the two terms appeared together in the old investigation. From now on, however, the file entry point and card status can no longer be collapsed into the same conclusion.
